about.browser_title: About Pratima Jain | From Pharmacist to Learning Designer at TCS
about.search_description: Pratima Jain's path from pharmacist to learning experience designer and project lead at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), and why she calls herself a learning engineer in the making.

opening.heading: From pharmacist to learning designer.
opening.paragraph: I'm Pratima Jain, a learning experience designer and project lead at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) in Mumbai. I trained as a pharmacist, and for more than nine years I have helped life sciences teams learn.
opening.drawing_description: A child's drawing of a medicine capsule, an arrow, and a pencil.

story.heading: How I got here
paragraphs: I discovered my love for learning and for training people at the Youth Trainer's Academy in 2013, and again while coordinating training for the International Pharmaceutical Students' Federation. I was studying pharmacy and management at the time, but I already knew I wanted to work in learning and development.

The chance came earlier than I expected. I began my career in scientific marketing. When my first employer closed its India office in 2017, I took it as my opening and joined TCS as a trainer. I have been in learning ever since.

story.heading: A learning engineer in the making
paragraphs: A learning engineer builds AI agents, software and automations so that people don't have to learn the task in the first place. Take a firm that needs flyers in its own brand style. I would rather build it a marketing coach that knows the brand guidelines than teach everyone graphic design.

It is the shortest possible route to the business objective, with the human touch and the learning process still at the heart of it. I'm getting there one experiment at a time, which is why I call myself a learning engineer in the making.

ideas.browser_title: Ideas & Experiments: Learning Ecosystems, Reels and Learning Games | Pratima Jain
ideas.search_description: Six ideas on how people learn, from learning ecosystems to microlearning vs reels, and three experiments, including a financial literacy game, by learning experience designer Pratima Jain.

opening.heading: Ideas and experiments on how people learn.
opening.paragraph: Most of my ideas start somewhere ordinary: a café counter, a family festival, a child's latest obsession. Here is why I would build learning ecosystems before courses, what separates microlearning from reels, and what I am making to test all of it.
opening.photo_description: Pratima Jain in a pink blazer, concentrating as she types on a laptop at a wooden table.

ideas.label: Idea 01
ideas.title: Learning ecosystems over courses
paragraphs: I once watched a child build their own curriculum around something they loved. Nobody sequenced it. There was video, play, things to hold, a book to look things up in, audio, and people who already cared about the subject. Each one came at the same world from a different angle, and the angles compounded.

A course is a delivery: one modality, one sitting, one format. Then we wonder why nothing holds three weeks later. I think L&D teams should stop shipping courses and start assembling learning ecosystems, accelerated with AI. Same budget, different unit of work.

ideas.label: Idea 02
ideas.title: Microlearning vs reels: attention is the entry fee, not the outcome
paragraphs: I have learnt from reels for years. So what separates a video in an e-learning module from a reel? If the module is only the video, nothing.

The video was never the learning. The learning is what we build around it: the sequence, the practice, the feedback when you get it wrong, the context of your role, and some proof that something changed.
ideas.quote: Reels get you to watch. Our job is to get you to do.

ideas.label: Idea 03
ideas.title: Learn the learner's five words
paragraphs: I don't learn a language to speak it well. I learn it to meet people where they are. A handful of words is enough to start a friendship.
That is the whole job of a learning designer. Learners don't need us to bring more words. They need us to learn theirs.

ideas.label: Idea 04
ideas.title: One workshop changes nothing on its own
paragraphs: One AI workshop or one course won't change anything unless the plan includes your day-to-day work. A good session gives people somewhere to start. What happens afterwards matters just as much.

ideas.label: Idea 05
ideas.title: A room gives you people
paragraphs: I make it to a few events a year, and the return is rarely the sessions. It is the people I meet on the way in and on the way out.
ideas.quote: A feed gives you information. A room gives you people.
ideas.after_quote: Those connections are what change how I think and what I do next.

ideas.label: Idea 06
ideas.title: Stakeholder management starts at home
paragraphs: A joint family is a large organisation. A nuclear family is a startup. In a startup you are agile, and you also sort everything out yourself. In a large organisation there are processes, and there is a backup for every emergency.

Life in a large household has taught me about competing interests, non-negotiables, and relationships that have to outlive the outcome. I do stakeholder management for a living, and I learnt a good part of it at home.
